narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the law school decided to reject your application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were your class ranking in your third year, your LSAT score, and your first-year class ranking. Your third-year ranking was by far the strongest influence and pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) in your final year of law school, compared with an average of roughly 6 among accepted students, signaled to the model that you struggled significantly toward the end of your studies. This was the main reason for the high risk estimate.

Your LSAT score of 37 worked in the opposite direction. It is almost exactly the same as the average for students who were accepted, so it helped pull the prediction slightly toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive effect was not strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

Your first-year ranking in the second decile also contributed to the failure prediction, though less strongly than your third-year performance. It showed that your academic standing started below average and remained low.

Given these results, the clearest next step is to focus on strengthening the areas that hurt your profile the most. Consider retaking key courses, seeking academic support, or gaining additional legal experience before reapplying. Improving your upper-level academic record would likely have the biggest impact on future predictions. (218 words)
